italian-game.name: The Italian
italian-game.summary: The oldest attacking opening: the bishop on c4 looks at f7, and the center is taken with c3 and d4.

notes.4: The bishop on c4: it looks at Black's weakest square, f7.
notes.6: c3 prepares d4 without losing the center.
notes.10: White got his pawn back and his center is stronger.

italian-game.planW: Take the center with c3 and d4, castle quickly, and then attack on the kingside with Re1 and Nbd2-f1-g3.
italian-game.planB: Pressure White's center with d5 at the right time, or play the quiet version with d6 and Bb6.

ruy-lopez.name: The Spanish (Ruy Lopez)
ruy-lopez.summary: The deepest opening in chess: long pressure on Black from the first moves to the end of the game.

notes.4: The bishop threatens the knight that protects e5.
notes.5: a6 asks the bishop: will you take or retreat?
notes.10: Re1 protects e4 and prepares a mobile center.
notes.14: c3 prepares d4 and opens a path for the bishop to c2.

ruy-lopez.planW: Build your center with c3 and d4, reroute the knight b1-d2-f1-g3, and wait for the moment to strike on the kingside.
ruy-lopez.planB: Fortify e5, expand on the queenside with b5, and prepare the counter-strike d5.

sicilian-najdorf.name: The Sicilian Najdorf
sicilian-najdorf.summary: Kasparov's choice: full flexibility for Black and a counterattack on the queenside.

notes.1: The Sicilian: Black attacks the center from the wing.
notes.5: The Open Sicilian: White opened the center early.
notes.9: a6! The Najdorf: it stops pieces from landing on b5 and prepares b5 and e5.
notes.11: e5: Black kicks the knight out of the center.

sicilian-najdorf.planW: Attack on the kingside with f3, g4 and O-O-O, and use the d5 square.
sicilian-najdorf.planB: Counterattack with b5 and Bb7, pressure the c file, and think about d5 to break the center.

sicilian-dragon.name: The Sicilian Dragon
sicilian-dragon.summary: The bishop on g7 like a dragon: the most dangerous diagonal in chess and a war on both wings.

notes.9: The Dragon: the bishop goes to g7 on the long diagonal.
notes.12: f3 protects e4 and prepares the opposite-side castling attack.
notes.13: Qd2: White intends O-O-O and h4-h5.

sicilian-dragon.planW: Castle long, push h4-h5, trade off Black's dark-squared bishop with Bh6, and open the h file.
sicilian-dragon.planB: The bishop on g7 is your soul: don't trade it for free. Attack with Rc8 and a6-b5 and pressure c3.

french-defense.name: The French
french-defense.summary: A wall of pawns and a counterattack on its base: the defense of the patient and stubborn.

notes.1: e6: preparation for d5 from behind cover.
notes.5: Winawer: the bishop pins the knight and declares war.
notes.7: c5! The strike at the base of the pawn chain. The soul of the French.
notes.9: Black broke the pin and broke up White's pawns.

french-defense.planW: Use the space on the kingside: f4-f5 or an attack with h4, and watch the weakness of the dark squares.
french-defense.planB: Hit the d4 base with c5, Nc6 and Qb6, and in endgames White's broken structure will be held to account.

caro-kann.name: The Caro-Kann
caro-kann.summary: The safest defense against e4: a sound structure, a free bishop, and comfortable endgames.

notes.1: c6: preparing d5 without locking in the bishop.
notes.7: The bishop comes out of the wall before e6. This is the whole idea of the Caro-Kann.
notes.10: h4 attacks the bishop, and h6 opens a window for it on h7.

caro-kann.planW: Expand with h4-h5 or play the Advance version with e5, and sometimes pressure the weakness on d6.
caro-kann.planB: Keep developing calmly: e6, Nd7 and Ngf6, trade pieces, and your endgames are usually more comfortable.

queens-gambit.name: The Queen's Gambit
queens-gambit.summary: Strategic pressure from the first move: c4 besieges d5 and the fight is long and rich.

notes.2: The gambit: pressure on d5 with the wing pawn.
notes.3: Black declined and fortified his center with e6.
notes.6: The bishop pins the knight against the king.
notes.13: b6 prepares the bishop on b7 on the longest diagonal.

queens-gambit.planW: Control the c file, prepare to break through the center with e4, and pressure the tired d5 square.
queens-gambit.planB: Free your position with c5 or e5 at the right time, and get the white-squared bishop out of its prison with b6 and Bb7.

kings-indian.name: The King's Indian
kings-indian.summary: Black leaves the center, fortifies his king, and then blows everything up with one strike.

notes.2: Black isn't fighting for the center right now. Patience.
notes.5: The bishop on g7: a sniper on the long diagonal.
notes.11: e5! The blow everything else was preparing for.
notes.13: The center is closed, and now it's a war of the wings: Black with f5 and White with c5.

kings-indian.planW: Expand on the queenside with c5, and don't open the kingside for any reason.
kings-indian.planB: Prepare f5 with the knight on e7 or g8, and then the kingside attack with pawns: f5-f4 and g5-g4.

london-system.name: The London System
london-system.summary: The same setup against almost anything: the least memorizing and the most safety possible.

notes.2: The bishop comes out before e3 locks it in. The most important rule in the London.
notes.8: c3 supports d4 and prepares a safe home for the bishop.
notes.12: The bishop goes back to g3 instead of being traded, and keeps looking along the diagonal.

london-system.planW: Continue the setup: Bd3, O-O and Ne5, and then either e4 or an attack on the kingside with Qf3 and h4.
london-system.planB: Hit the center with c5 or e5, and trade off the London dark-squared bishop if you can.

english-opening.name: The English
english-opening.summary: c4: control of d5 from the wing, and flexibility that lets you transpose into any system.

notes.0: The English: White controls d5 without a center pawn.
notes.4: It looks like a reversed Sicilian: White has an extra move.
notes.6: The fianchetto supports the center from afar.

english-opening.planW: Control d5 with pieces, not pawns, and pressure the queenside with Rb1 and b4.
english-opening.planB: Hold the center with d5 or play quietly with d6 and g6, and watch out for the b4-b5 pressure.

scandinavian.name: The Scandinavian
scandinavian.summary: d5 in the face of e4 from the first move: direct, solid, and easy to learn.

notes.1: The challenge from the first move: d5!
notes.3: The queen takes back the pawn. Its only drawback: the queen will be chased.
notes.5: Qa5: the safe place for the queen, and from there she pressures the wing.
notes.11: c6 protects d5 and opens an exit for the queen.

scandinavian.planW: Gain time by chasing the queen with Nc3 and Bd2, and keep developing fast.
scandinavian.planB: Develop calmly: Bf5 or Bg4, e6, Nbd7, and don't rush the queen back again.

pirc-defense.name: The Pirc
pirc-defense.summary: Leave the center to White and besiege it: the defense of the cunning with cool nerves.

notes.2: Black lets White take the whole center.
notes.6: The fianchetto: the bishop on g7 besieges the center from afar.
notes.11: Bg4 pressures d4 through the knight.

pirc-defense.planW: Take the center, but don't push all the pawns early: every push leaves weak squares behind.
pirc-defense.planB: Besiege the center with pieces, and strike it with e5 or c5 when ready, and the kingside isn't for show.

kings-gambit.name: The King's Gambit
kings-gambit.summary: The boldest opening in history: the f4 pawn is a gift to break the center and attack f7 before Black can breathe.

notes.2: f4: the gambit. White gives a pawn in return for the center and the attack.
notes.3: Black accepted the challenge and took the pawn.
notes.5: g5: Black tries to keep the loot by force.
notes.8: Ne5! The knight at the center of the attack: the King's Gambit square.
notes.13: The position is on fire: White has development and a center, and Black holds an extra pawn but is undeveloped.

kings-gambit.planW: Develop at lightning speed, open the f file, and aim everything at f7. If Black clings to the pawn, he'll be choked in development.
kings-gambit.planB: Give the pawn back at the right time (usually d5) and continue your development: whoever holds onto the loot to the end loses the game.

queens-indian.name: The Queen's Indian
queens-indian.summary: A calm and solid defense: the bishop on b7 besieges e4 from afar without Black putting a pawn in the center.

notes.5: b6: the bishop will come out on the longest diagonal on the board, a8-h1.
notes.7: Bb7 besieges e4 and keeps White from expanding easily.
notes.13: Ne4! Occupying the center with pieces, not pawns: the philosophy of the Indian school.
notes.16: Black continued his development soundly and there isn't a single weakness in his camp.

queens-indian.planW: Expand in the center with e4 if you can, or play on the queenside with b4 and a4.
queens-indian.planB: Control e4, clarify the pieces with no future, and then attack White's center with d5 or c5.

slav-defense.name: The Slav Defense
slav-defense.summary: The most solid reply to the Queen's Gambit: c6 protects d5 without locking in the bishop, and Black always comes out with sound pieces.

notes.3: c6: the support for d5. The c8 bishop stays free - the Slav's advantage over the ordinary defense.
notes.7: dxc4: Black takes the gambit seriously.
notes.9: Bf5: the bishop came out before e6, and if it had waited it would have been locked in.
notes.12: White got his pawn back but Black stands solid as a rock.

slav-defense.planW: Use your space in the center, and prepare e4 or play on the half-open c file.
slav-defense.planB: Continue your development in peace, and then break the center with c5 or e5 at the moment your pieces are ready.

scotch-game.name: The Scotch
scotch-game.summary: A direct and honest opening: `d4` on move three opens the game early and gives White a mobile center and free pieces.

notes.4: **d4!** The immediate strike: instead of maneuvering, White opens the center right away.
notes.7: **...Bc5** Black replies with attacking development - the game becomes open and fun.
notes.9: **...Qf6** A famous idea: pressure on the `d4` knight and the `f2` pawn at the same time.
notes.13: The center is broken and all the pieces are free: the Scotch gives an open game without the complexity of the Italian.

scotch-game.planW: Open the center early with d4, develop with checks and pressure on f7, and use the extra space before Black pulls himself together.
scotch-game.planB: Meet the center with a center: d5 at the right time frees your pieces, and don't be afraid of trades - the position is equal but alive.

grunfeld-defense.name: The Grünfeld
grunfeld-defense.summary: The defense of the rebels: Black lets White build a huge pawn center, and then demolishes it with long-range piece pressure on the big diagonal.

notes.5: **...d5!** The direct challenge: the Grünfeld isn't a diplomatic defense.
notes.9: **...Nxc3** gives White the dream center d4-e4... in appearance only.
notes.11: **...Bg7** The bishop on the big diagonal a1-h8: the Grünfeld's secret weapon that will hit the whole center.
notes.15: **...c5** The counterattack begins: every white center pawn becomes a target, not a strength.
notes.23: **...Na5** The knight heads for c4: the Grünfeld turns from a defense into a full counterattack.

grunfeld-defense.planW: Keep your center and complete it in peace: d5 at the right moment gains space, but every extra advance creates a target.
grunfeld-defense.planB: Let them build the center and then tear it down: pressure with Bg7, c5, Nc6 and Bg4 - when a huge center falls, it falls all at once.

petrov-defense.name: Petrov's Defense
petrov-defense.summary: The calm Russian defense: Black attacks the `e4` pawn at once instead of defending `e5` - an equal game without complexity.

notes.3: **...Nf6!** Attack is the best defense: Black attacks the `e4` pawn right away.
notes.5: **...d6** Patience first: the immediate capture `...Nxe4` too early would have given White the initiative.
notes.7: **...Nxe4** Now the capture is safe: the game is completely equal.
notes.13: **...Be7** Calm development: the Petrov isn't about attack, it's about solidity.
notes.17: A comfortable position for Black: a draw isn't a defeat, and White has to justify his initiative.

petrov-defense.planW: Press on `e5` and try to create a kingside attack with `c4` and `Re1`, but the position leans toward a draw if Black is accurate.
petrov-defense.planB: Be accurate in development and don't rush to capture: `...d6` first, and then `...Nxe4` safely. An equal game against a player stronger than you is a win.

nimzo-indian.name: The Nimzo-Indian
nimzo-indian.summary: The most refined defense against `d4`: the bishop pressures `c3` and doubles the pawns - a strategic battle between structure and the two bishops.

notes.5: **...Bb4!** The Nimzo: it stops `e4` by pressuring the knight, not with pawns.
notes.11: **...c5** The strike at the center: everything in the Nimzo revolves around `d4` and `e4`.
notes.15: **...Bxc3** The historic deal: Black gives a bishop in return for doubling White's pawns - a permanent weakness.
notes.19: **...Qc7** The queen pressures the doubled pawns: a long-term target for the big games.

nimzo-indian.planW: Keep your bishops and strike in the center quickly before the weakness is felt: the Nimzo becomes critical if White falls behind.
nimzo-indian.planB: Trade `...Bxc3` at the moment you double the pawns, and then besiege and pressure them: patience eats the center slowly.

vienna-game.name: The Vienna
vienna-game.summary: The cunning opening: `Nc3` looks calm, and then tactical surprises on the kingside catch even the strongest players.

notes.2: **Nc3** The Vienna: White hides his intentions - no obvious `Nf3` and no early `Bc4`.
notes.5: **...Nxe4** Black thinks he's won a pawn...
notes.6: **Qh5!** The surprise: the queen attacks and the knight is poisoned.
notes.10: **Nb5!** The threat of a check on `c7`: the Vienna turns from calm to a storm in one move.
notes.16: **Nxc7+** The royal check: the `a8` rook falls and Black has no castling.
notes.18: The knight looks odd on `a8` but White has won material and the initiative: the Vienna rewards boldness.

vienna-game.planW: Play it cunningly: develop calmly and then strike fast on the kingside with `f4` or `Bc4` - the relaxed Black gets surprised.
vienna-game.planB: Reply with `...d5` early or play the solid version `...Nc6` and `...Bb4`, and watch out for `Qh5` if you plan to take `e4`.

catalan.name: The Catalan
catalan.summary: The opening of world championships: your bishop on the big diagonal pressures the queenside all game - a delicious, slow poison.

notes.4: **g3** The whole idea of the Catalan: the bishop goes to `g2` and looks along the longest diagonal on the board.
notes.7: **...dxc4** Black takes the pawn - and White leaves it for now, trusting the diagonal.
notes.14: **Qxc4** The pawn comes back with interest: the pressure on `b7` and `a8` remains.
notes.19: **...Be4** Black tries to close the diagonal: the real Catalan battle has begun. A typical position from here: long-term pressure for White, and accurate defense required from Black.

catalan.planW: Don't rush: the pressure of the `g2` bishop grows with time. Free the rooks onto open files and pressure the queenside.
catalan.planB: Close the diagonal with `...Be4` and `...c6`, and free yourself with `...c5` at the right moment before the pressure chokes you.

alekhine-defense.name: Alekhine's Defense
alekhine-defense.summary: Provocation itself: Black makes White's pawns chase his knight until they overextend, and then strikes them. The opening of the fourth world champion.

notes.1: **...Nf6!** Alekhine's Defense: Black lures White's pawns to advance and overextend so he can strike them later.
notes.8: **f4** The four pawns attack: the fiercest reply to Alekhine, and White's center looks frightening.
notes.21: **...f6!** The counter-strike prepared from the start: breaking the advanced center.
notes.23: The position is equal: White's center has been broken but development makes the difference, and Black is solid and ready for the middlegame.

alekhine-defense.planW: Don't overextend carelessly: develop behind your pawns and keep your center, and use the `d6` square if Black miscalculates.
alekhine-defense.planB: Provoke and strike: besiege the advanced pawns with `...d6` and `...f6`, and keep your pieces pressuring `d4` and `e5` until the center falls.

dutch-defense.name: The Dutch
dutch-defense.summary: The fighting reply to `d4`: Black takes control of the `e4` square by force from the first move and builds a kingside attack - sometimes at the expense of his king's safety.

notes.1: **...f5** The Dutch: Black takes control of `e4` by force from the first move.
notes.7: **...d5** The Stonewall: a rock in the center, but the `c8` bishop becomes Black's chronic problem.
notes.17: **...Ne4** The central knight: the soul of the Dutch and the key to its attack on the king.
notes.21: A battle of open squares: Black holds `e4` and White looks for weak dark squares around the Stonewall.

dutch-defense.planW: Besiege the Stonewall: trade off the bad `g2` bishop against `d6`, and pressure the dark squares (`e5` especially) and the locked-in `c8` bishop.
dutch-defense.planB: Build the Stonewall with patience (`...d5` `...c6`), focus your knight on `e4`, and solve the `c8` bishop problem early with `...b6` or `...Bd7-e8-h5`.

reti-opening.name: The Réti
reti-opening.summary: An opening of the hypermodern school: White besieges the center from afar with pieces and a fianchettoed bishop, and strikes it at the right moment.

notes.0: **Nf3** The Réti: maximum flexibility, and White reveals his intentions very slowly.
notes.2: **c4** Pressure on `d5` from the wing: the essence of the hypermodern school - besiege the center instead of occupying it.
notes.22: **e4** The central explosion: the Réti turns into a real war at exactly the right time.
notes.29: **...c5** Black's natural reply: a counter-strike on the center, and a lively position for both sides.

reti-opening.planW: Besiege from afar and strike on time: two bishops on the long diagonals, safe castling, and an `e4` explosion when all your pieces are ready.
reti-opening.planB: Build a solid wall with `...c6` and `...e6`, develop calmly, and hit the center with `...c5` or `...dxc4` when White overextends.

benoni-defense.name: The Modern Benoni
benoni-defense.summary: The fiercest reply to `d4`: Black sells space in return for a merciless counterattack on the queenside and the big diagonal. The opening of Fischer and Tal.

notes.3: **...c5** The Benoni: an immediate challenge to the center pawn, and Black accepts an advanced white center in return for sharp counterplay.
notes.11: **...g6** The bishop goes to `g7`: from the big diagonal it will look at the `b2` pawn and the half-open `e` file.
notes.23: **...Rb8** The classic preparation for `...b5`: breaking open the queenside is the dream of every Benoni player.
notes.27: **...Nh5** The knight heads toward `f4`: Black attacks on both wings, and White has to win before he's crushed.

benoni-defense.planW: Use the space: pressure the weak `d6` pawn, tighten your grip on `c4` and `e4`, and don't give Black the chance for `...b5` for free.
benoni-defense.planB: Counterattack is a way of life: the `g7` bishop, pressure on the `e` file, `...a6` and `...b5`, and an active knight on `e5`. Don't play it if you like quiet.

philidor-defense.name: Philidor's Defense
philidor-defense.summary: Solidity first: Black builds a small tight wall and waits for White to overextend. The opening of Philidor, who said "pawns are the soul of chess".

notes.3: **...d6** Philidor: protecting `e5` with the pawn, not the knight, and a solid wall from day one.
notes.13: **...c6** The wall is completed: Black is entrenched in a small but tight house.
notes.19: **...d5!** The central strike: when the fortification is complete, Black breaks the center and frees his pieces.
notes.23: The position is nearly equal: Black solved all his problems without giving White any target.

philidor-defense.planW: Don't rush to break the wall: keep developing, take space quietly (`a4` for example), and pressure the `e5` point until Black is forced to resolve it on your terms.
philidor-defense.planB: Patience is your weapon: fortify `e5`, develop behind the wall, and then strike with `...d5` or `...exd4` at a time that suits you. The wall isn't surrender, it's tactics.
